findings.passage: In 2019 the actor Elliot Page had criticized his church as anti-LGBTQ.
findings.problem: Pratt's public answer to the charge is missing. The paragraph gives Page's criticism, the Zoe pastor's 2017 film and the Daily Beast's 'Lying' headline, but never what Pratt said in 2019. Men's Health 2022, already cited, quotes his statement: "Nothing could be further from the truth. I am a man who believes that everyone is entitled to love who they want free from the judgment of their fellow man." TheWrap (February 2019, opened for this review) carries the fuller Instagram text ("no church defines me or my life", "We need less hate in this world, not more"). Even the Daily Beast concedes he "refuted Page's allegations." Evidence claim c-page-criticism says "his response is given in the next sentence", but the next sentence is the 2022 Hillsong denial. Two sentences later, "Asked why he hadn't set the record straight at the time" makes it look as if he stayed silent in 2019. In Men's Health the question ("Why not say that at the time?") was only about not saying he had never been to Hillsong. The draft also drops his immediate qualification: "If it's like the Westboro Baptist Church, that's different." Readers come away thinking he never answered an anti-LGBTQ charge.
findings.acceptance_test: Directly after Page's criticism, the paragraph gives Pratt's dated 2019 response. At minimum it quotes "Nothing could be further from the truth" and the "entitled to love who they want" sentence, sourced to Men's Health 2022 or the 2019 statement. The "at the time" question is limited to Hillsong attendance (for example, "Asked why he hadn't said in 2019 that he had never attended Hillsong"). evidence-edit records the response as a claim with its source. The paragraph's net word count stays roughly level.

findings.passage: His account has shifted with the setting.
findings.problem: This sentence says he tells different audiences different things. The evidence's own inference for c-faith-by-room says the same ("shifts with the audience"), but the paragraph never shows it. Its example, "really I'm not a religious person", rests on a religion-versus-faith distinction he draws consistently. The draft's own FAQ treats it as a consistent line, and the Daily Beast calls that distinction "common amongst younger, modern Christians." What the record actually shows is change over time. His church went from Zoe (2019), to Zoe "not exclusively" with a Catholic baptism (2022), to a Catholic prayer-app partnership (2025). His view of the 2018 speech went from "Maybe it was hubris... I'm not sure I touched anybody" (Men's Health 2022) to "I didn't backtrack... I'm not going to apologize for that" (Not Dead Yet 2026). The draft also lets the Daily Beast's "Lying" headline stand as the representative response without saying the piece is opinion commentary. Separately, the evidence record understates the Daily Beast's 2017 Hillsong-photo claim. The article links "previously photographed" to a Yahoo report (September 14, 2017; photo credited BACKGRID/Splash News) of Pratt at a Wednesday service at Hillsong's Los Angeles location. c-hillsong-photo ("names no photographer, agency or event") and the matching research task are out of date.
findings.acceptance_test: Remove "shifted with the setting" and any other wording implying he tailors his faith account to the audience. Restore it only if the paragraph shows two dated statements to different audiences that actually conflict. A dated change-over-time contrast (for example, 2022 "hubris" versus 2026 "I didn't backtrack") may replace it, framed as a change, not as dishonesty. Identify the Daily Beast piece as opinion or commentary. Source the photo to the contemporaneous September 2017 report and its agency credit rather than to the opinion piece alone, and state that Pratt has not addressed that photo in the sources opened. Update c-hillsong-photo and its research task to match.

findings.passage: Eleven years later he wants the fun back, and he has said what made it easy. The funny guy didn't have to be hurt.
findings.problem: The closing presents a pain-avoidance motive for a current career decision as fact, and it gets there through two slides. First, the 2015 "fun" was his off-screen persona in the heavy years ("That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay", GQ). The 2026 "fun and lightheartedness" is about choosing comedic roles (Not Dead Yet). "He wants the fun back" joins the two and implies he wants the 2015 mask back. Second, Schur's "main character dilemma" is a craft point: leads need an arc ("They need to be vulnerable. They need to be hurt"). "The funny guy didn't have to be hurt" moves that point from the character Andy onto Pratt himself. His own stated reasons get no place in the conclusion: his recent roles were serious, comedy is "something I have," and his priority is now "being present at home" and working close to home (Not Dead Yet, 45:57 to 48:31). He also said that in the comedy years "people really responded well to it" (The Playlist). The evidence entry c-closing-interp sets no limit on this transfer.
findings.acceptance_test: Keep the jazz-soloist material. Mark any claim about why he wants comedy now as interpretation (for example, "this suggests"), and place at least one of his own stated reasons beside it. Make "didn't have to be hurt" clearly about the role (for example, "Andy never had to be hurt"), not about Pratt. Do not present the 2015 off-screen image and the 2026 role preference as the same "fun." Keep the change roughly word-neutral.

findings.passage: His road rage lasted one clause.
findings.problem: This misstates GQ 2015. Pratt told Chris Heath he was "so mad" that "It cost me twenty minutes." He also said he fed the anger on purpose as acting research ("Just get mad. Just get fucking pissed..."). Only when Heath asked about the incident again did his retelling flip ("No, I'm sure she didn't. It was probably my fault..."). Heath reads the same story as showing "how fiercely, and not so far beneath Pratt's abundant charm and warmth, anger is bubbling away," which is the opposite of the draft's use. The earlier line "The anger lasted one clause before he talked himself out of it and blamed his wandering mind." carries the same distortion in softer form. The anecdote counts as evidence against Type 8 and for the Seven reframe, so the error reaches the type argument.
findings.acceptance_test: Both passages match what GQ reports: the anger lasted the drive (about twenty minutes), he fed it deliberately as acting research, and the reversal came in his retelling to the interviewer. Delete "His road rage lasted one clause" or rewrite it to say his retelling flipped within one answer. If the anecdote stays in "Why not Type 8, 6 or 9?", acknowledge Heath's contrary reading. Update c-road-rage-interp.

findings.passage: A skeptic will add that faith audiences are a market too.
findings.problem: An unnamed skeptic, voiced by the author, suggests his faith has a commercial motive. The sentence follows the Hallow partnership, but the draft leaves out the reason Pratt gave for that partnership in the same Christian Post piece: "if I partner with Hallow, maybe I can amplify what is ultimately a really beautiful thing" and "That's why I partnered with Hallow." The standard requires disputed readings to be attributed and paired with relevant responses. c-faith-market cites only the Christian Post, which makes no such argument.
findings.acceptance_test: Either attribute the market reading to a named critic in an opened source (the Daily Beast's line about his "'proud Christian working in Hollywood' bit" would qualify) or cut the sentence. If it stays, his stated reason for the Hallow partnership appears in the same section. No net word gain.

findings.passage: Gunn told GQ that Pratt "didn't trust himself to just be Chris Pratt."
findings.problem: In the Three case this reads as a lasting third-party diagnosis of self-doubt. In GQ, Gunn is describing the first Guardians shoot, which Pratt says was hard for Gunn "for about the first half of the movie." Gunn explains it by Pratt's years as "the funny sidekick, which means that he always has to juggle to entertain everybody," and finishes with praise ("and how desirable that is to an audience"). In context, the quote supports the entertain-everybody reading at least as much as an image reading. c-gunn-juggle already notes the limit, but the prose does not.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence carries its time frame (the first Guardians shoot) or Gunn's sidekick clause, so readers see it as a remark about one adjustment on one film, not a standing trait.

findings.passage: A door-to-door sales venture had collapsed and left him in debt, and he had let his hometown believe it was going great.
findings.problem: The failure is framed as purely personal. Pratt's own accounts include the business model. On SmartLess (2022, auto-captions) he put the coupon company among "these multi-level marketing things". On Not Dead Yet (2026) he said the recruiting ad drew "the bottom of the unemployment barrel" ("people that like would go steal stuff and just disappear"). Vanity Fair's narration says he had "been caught in someone else's moneymaking scheme." Without that context, "definitely a failure" and the hidden-failure Three evidence read as more personal than his own telling. The "zero critical thinking skills" line used in the Six section comes from the same MLM answer and is a joke about his household (his mother would "believe anything anyone told her... sweet bless her heart"), yet it is offered as evidence of his adult temperament.
findings.acceptance_test: One attributed clause, at the first mention or in "What you're selling is yourself", says he later described the company as a multi-level-marketing scheme. The "zero critical thinking" line either keeps that context or is cut from the Six argument. Keep the change word-neutral.

findings.passage: The account holds steady across seven years of interviews, but it is his alone, and his father died in 2014.
findings.problem: Dan Pratt, a private person who has died, appears only through his son's harshest lines: boxer, bouncer, "mean", and acted like he disliked his son. The opened sources also carry Pratt's own more complex lines. In Vanity Fair 2017: "I think it made him proud, and it was cool that I got to find some way to connect with him, because he was a hard man to connect with." In 2026 (Not Dead Yet; Fox News) he said he wants to get right everything his dad got right as well as what he got wrong. He also describes the father's MS from his high-school years and "the bank takes our house away" (Not Dead Yet). The next line, "The family ran on hope more than on security," keeps the dreamers half of that answer and drops its other half: "we had to be survivors... we didn't have a pot to piss in."
findings.acceptance_test: The father passage adds one short line of Pratt's own warmer or more balanced account (VF 2017 or 2026). It also adds either the illness and lost-house context or the "survivors" half of the dreamers answer. Add no new psychological claim about the father, record the added material in evidence-edit, and keep the addition short given the length.

findings.passage: from James Reese in _The Terminal List_
findings.problem: The character is James Reece (Men's Health 2022: "he inhabits James Reece"; Jack Carr's novels). "Reese" is a homophone from the machine transcript, and the evidence claim text repeats it.
findings.acceptance_test: "James Reece" in the body and in the matching evidence claim text.

protected_passages.passage: Both accounts are his. Side by side, they show a move that runs through his life: he meets a bad stretch by finding the fun in it, first while living it and again when he tells the story.
protected_passages.reason: Separates his two retellings (the record) from the article's reading (interpretation) right at the hook, which is the separation the standard asks for.

protected_passages.passage: In Vanity Fair's reconstruction of his telling, he answered, "Fuck, yeah, I act. Put me in a movie."
protected_passages.reason: Labels reconstructed dialogue as the magazine's reconstruction instead of passing it off as verbatim speech.

protected_passages.passage: Here the Three and Seven readings split. People of every type hide a failure, so the hiding settles little.
protected_passages.reason: States an unflattering fact (he hid the failure) without moralizing and refuses to let it carry the typing on its own.

protected_passages.passage: The limits are real. Most of the Seven evidence is his own retelling in interviews, the cleanest test came when he was about 19, and the "pure euphoria" line comes from auto-captions of a podcast. A reader can still argue Three.
protected_passages.reason: Gives honest inference limits in the body, where the reader meets the argument, not in a footer.

protected_passages.passage: Even so, more than a decade of public faith, held through the mockery, is the strand of Pratt the type explains least.
protected_passages.reason: Treats his faith as a real, costly commitment the type does not explain rather than as a symptom. Keep it even if the sentence before it changes.

assessment: Fairness-proxy read. The draft mostly keeps what Pratt said separate from what it infers. It flags reconstructed dialogue and caption-only lines and names his faith as the strand the type explains least. The fairness problems cluster in the faith/LGBTQ paragraph and the ending. His 2019 answer to the anti-LGBTQ charge is missing (subject-01). "Shifted with the setting" accuses him of audience-tailoring that the sources do not show, and an opinion headline goes unlabeled (subject-02). The last line reads a pain-avoidance motive into a current career choice and merges a lead character's arc with the man (subject-03). The GQ road-rage anecdote is misstated in both places it appears (subject-04). Smaller gaps are an unattributed 'market' insinuation, a time-bound Gunn quote, missing MLM context, a one-sided portrait of his late father, and a misspelled character name. Sources reopened for this review: saved copies of Men's Health 2022, GQ 2015, Vanity Fair 2017 (both copies), The Christian Post 2025, Fox News 2026 and The Playlist 2026; the Daily Beast 2022 via a fresh Wayback raw fetch (full text with its links); the Not Dead Yet Whisper transcript; and the SmartLess and Club Random captions. Two sources outside the record were also opened: TheWrap's February 2019 report of his Instagram statement and the Yahoo report of September 14, 2017 that the Daily Beast links for the Hillsong photo. Similarity tripped mainly on this page's own 2026-10-29 version (self-matches). The Florence Pugh ('anticipating what comes next', 'gut instinct') and Dominic Fike ('gets a full hearing below') matches are stock type and structure phrases, not reused arguments, so there is no finding. The body is about 3,830 words against the 3,500 target, so fixes should be close to word-neutral. Every research risk flag stays on (sensitive allegations, contested typing, the 3-to-7 thesis change), so the six-role jury applies.
